engine.title: The multibagger screen qualified nobody for four weeks
engine.body: Corrects what this entry said on 2026-08-27. It read ‘the scan is running on schedule’ and blamed the fixed list on cadence. The ledger says otherwise: the last multibagger row is 2026-08-01, while magic, magicmagic and ai_longterm — the same Saturday job, the same slot — all logged 2026-08-22. Twenty-six days, three Saturdays, nothing written.
engine.note: The screen is not broken. Run on 2026-08-27 it took 11 candidates and rejected 10 for R:R below 2.0 — CHENNPETRO 1.29, FLUOROCHEM 1.07, GLAXO 0.59, which needs a 63% win rate merely to break even. The defect was that a week qualifying nobody wrote nothing at all, so the page served the 1 August list as though it were current. The attempt is recorded either way now. The gate is NOT loosened: publishing a 0.59 R:R to keep the section busy is the exact trade this screen exists to refuse, and an empty week is a real result.

engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Thinking Process
chess.body: Every move: 1. What did my opponent just do? (threats?) 2. What are my candidate moves? (at least 2-3) 3. Calculate each candidate 2-3 moves deep. 4. Use LPDO check. 5. Make the move. Don't play on impulse. Even 30 seconds of structured thinking eliminates 80% of blunders. This process is the difference between 800 and 1200 Elo.

wisdom.title: The Identity Question
wisdom.body: Who are you when the job title is gone, when the market is closed, when your daughter is asleep? Define yourself by what you do, not what you've achieved. 'I am someone who learns daily. I love deeply. I show up.' These don't depend on AED 30K or a Dubai visa. They're yours now.

book.author: Morgan Housel
book.lesson: In investing and in life, a small number of events account for the majority of outcomes. Venture capital funds know that 1 investment out of 50 will return the entire fund. Amazon's success is almost entirely explained by AWS — which started as an internal experiment. Housel's lesson: you can be wrong most of the time and still be enormously successful if you're right on the few things that matter most. This means long tail bets matter. Staying in the game long enough to hit the tails matters. Avoiding ruin so you can be there for the rare extraordinary outcomes matters most.
book.key_quote: You only need to be right a few times in your life, as long as you don't catastrophically lose the ability to keep playing.
book.action: Identify the two or three decisions in your career/portfolio that would be truly transformative. Optimise for those, not the daily noise.
crux: Doing well with money has little to do with intelligence and everything to do with behaviour.
No one is crazy. Every money decision makes sense given that person's specific history of experience.
Luck and risk are the shadow siblings of every outcome. Neither is measurable, both are decisive.
There is no reason to risk what you have for what you don't need.
Compounding is counterintuitive: $81.5bn of Buffett's $84.5bn arrived after his 65th birthday.
Getting money and keeping money are different skills. The second requires frugality and paranoia.
Tails drive everything. A minority of events account for the majority of outcomes.
The highest dividend money pays is control over your own time.
Wealth is what you don't see. Spending is evidence of spending, not of wealth.
Save without a specific goal. Savings buy optionality against a world you cannot forecast.
Room for error is the single most underrated force. Plan for the plan not going to plan.
Avoid extreme financial commitments — your future self's goals will not match your current ones.
Volatility is the fee for high returns, not a fine for a mistake. Fees you pay willingly; fines you avoid.
Define the game you are playing, and stop taking cues from people playing a different one.
learnings: A mediocre strategy held for 30 years beats a brilliant one abandoned in year 3.
Most financial mistakes are emotional, so most financial fixes must be behavioural.
Survival is the prerequisite for compounding. Everything else is secondary.
Your risk tolerance is not a number. It is what you actually do at a 40% drawdown.
examples: Ronald Read, a petrol-station attendant, left $8m by buying blue chips for decades. Richard Fuscone, Harvard MBA and Merrill executive, went bankrupt in 2008.
Bill Gates went to one of the only high schools on earth with a computer in 1968 — one in a million odds. His equally able friend Kent Evans died climbing.
Buffett's returns are good but not historically unique; his 80-year runway is. Start at 30 instead of 10 and the fortune largely disappears.
adapt: SIP ₹5–15K/month for the BMW fund. The consistency matters more than the monthly amount.
Keep 6 months of KL expenses liquid before scaling any trading capital. Room for error first.
Trading capital is separate from family capital. Never one pool.
The Dubai target is AED 30K/month, not 'as much as possible'. Define enough or the goalpost moves forever.

interview_tech.q: Gross margin fell 180bps. Walk me through the bridge.
interview_tech.a: Decompose into four drivers: mix — did the sales split shift toward lower-margin categories; price — did you discount more, measured as markdown as a percent of gross sales; cost — did landed cost rise from FX, freight or supplier price; and shrink/wastage. Quantify each in basis points so they sum to 180. The bridge is the answer, not the total. In retail the most common culprit is markdown depth on aged stock, which is really an buying error surfacing one season late.

interview_tech.q: Auditors propose an adjustment you disagree with. What do you do?
interview_tech.a: Separate judgement from fact. If it is a factual error, show the evidence and it goes away. If it is a judgement — provisioning, impairment, lease term — set out your basis in a technical memo: the standard, the specific paragraph, the assumptions and their support. Escalate to the engagement partner if needed, and involve the audit committee chair early rather than late. If they still disagree and it is material, you record it. What you never do is trade an adjustment against a different one.

interview_soft.q: What questions do you have for us?
interview_soft.a: Never none. Ask things that reveal you are evaluating them: what does the first 12 months look like for whoever takes this; what is the finance function currently not able to answer that the board keeps asking; how is the relationship between finance and the commercial teams today; and why is the role open. The last one is the most informative and the least asked. Avoid salary and benefits at first interview.

interview_soft.q: Describe a situation where you had incomplete information and had to decide anyway.
interview_soft.a: Forecasting and provisioning are full of these. Structure: what you knew, what you could not know in the time available, the cost of waiting, the assumption you took and why, and how you made the assumption visible rather than burying it. The mark of seniority is deciding with 70% of the information and saying explicitly what would change your mind — say that phrase.

cfo_field.q: Know your break-even by store, not by chain.
cfo_field.a: A chain at group-level profitability can be carrying a quarter of its estate below contribution. Compute store contribution — gross profit less rent, staff and directly attributable fixed cost — and rank it. Then, before closing anything: is the lease committed, what does the store contribute to online fulfilment in its catchment, and what is the exit cost. A negative-contribution store with four years left on a non-cancellable lease is usually cheaper to run than to close.
cfo_field.who: The analysis that gets you noticed

cfo_field.q: VAT in the GCC is a cash-flow instrument, not just a compliance task.
cfo_field.a: Registration thresholds, filing frequency and the timing of input recovery all move working capital. A group filing quarterly rather than monthly holds recoverable input VAT longer than it needs to. Know the filing calendar in every jurisdiction the group trades in, and know which entity holds the recoverable balance — a refund stuck in the wrong entity is cash you own and cannot use.

lichess_games.analysis: Focus on early king safety: castle by move 7, avoid leaving the king in the center past move 10.
lichess_games.standout: Decided on the clock, not the board — the position was still playable when time ran out.

lichess_summary.session_summary: You’re crushing opponents but you never leave the opening book—your “weakest opening” is a blank, meaning you haven’t even tested alternatives, so you’re vulnerable to anyone who knows the theory. Stop relying on rote memorization and spend 30 minutes each day drilling the first 10 moves of at least two contrasting defenses (e.g., Sicilian Najdorf and Caro‑Kann) until you can play them without hesitation. Then schedule weekly blitz games where you must start each match with one of those lines; review every loss to pinpoint where the opening crumbled and adjust immediately.

lichess_puzzle.tip: King activity and pawn structure dominate. Technique over tactics here.
